items.title: Magic Pak
items.text:
The building is not equipped with a centralized heating and cooling system. Heating and cooling within individual suites are provided by in suite MagicPak units, which consist of a gas fired furnace for space heating and an integral DX cooling section for space cooling, operating independently in each suite.
While this decentralized configuration provides basic temperature control, gas fired furnace and conventional DX cooling systems are generally less efficient than heat pump solutions. Typical non-condensing gas furnaces operate at thermal efficiencies in the range of 78–82%, while standard DX cooling sections often achieve cooling COP values of approximately 2.8–3.5, depending on equipment age and condition. In comparison, modern high efficiency air source heat pump (ASHP) systems can achieve heating and cooling COP values exceeding 4.0–5.0 under favorable conditions.
In addition to moderate energy performance, the distributed nature of MagicPak units increases overall maintenance and lifecycle costs, as each suite contains its own combustion appliance, heat exchanger, blower motor, and refrigeration components. Annual servicing, combustion inspections, heat exchanger monitoring, and potential component replacement contribute to higher long-term operating expenses compared to mini-split heat pump systems.
Given the age and inherent efficiency limitations of gas fired packaged units, replacement with a mini-split heat pump system should be considered in the short term as part of a mechanical system modernization strategy to improve energy efficiency, reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and lower long-term maintenance and operating costs

items.title: PTAC (Packaged Terminal Air Conditioner)
items.text:
Heating and cooling within individual suites are provided by in-suite PTAC (Packaged Terminal Air Conditioner) units, which provide electric resistance heating and DX cooling.

PTAC systems offer basic suite-level temperature control; however, they are significantly less efficient than modern heat pump–based systems. Typical PTAC units operate with cooling COP values in the range of approximately 2.5–3.2, while electric-resistance heating sections operate at a COP of approximately 1.0, meaning that one unit of electrical energy produces one unit of heat. By comparison, modern cold-climate air-source heat pump (ASHP) systems can achieve heating and cooling COP values exceeding 4.0 under favorable operating conditions, delivering substantially higher efficiency and lower operating costs.

As PTAC units age, cooling performance may decline due to compressor wear and refrigerant-related servicing requirements, and overall electrical consumption remains high during the heating season due to resistance-based heating.

Given the relatively low heating efficiency and increasing lifecycle costs associated with electric-resistance-based PTAC systems, replacement with a modern air-source heat pump (ASHP) system is recommended in the short term. Transitioning to ASHP technology would significantly improve energy performance, reduce electrical consumption, lower operating costs, and enhance long-term system reliability.

items.title: Electric Baseboard Heater
items.text:
The building is not equipped with a centralized hydronic or forced-air heating system. Space heating within individual suites is provided by in-suite electric resistance baseboard heaters, which operate independently in each unit and are controlled by local thermostats.

Electric resistance heating directly converts electrical energy into thermal energy and operates at an effective coefficient of performance (COP) of approximately 1.0. This means that one unit of electrical energy produces one unit of heat. While simple in design and relatively low in maintenance, electric baseboard systems are typically associated with higher operating costs compared to modern heat pump–based systems.

In comparison, high-efficiency air-source heat pump (ASHP) systems utilize a refrigeration cycle to transfer heat from the outdoor air into the building during the heating season. Modern ASHP systems can achieve seasonal heating COP values in the range of 3.0–4.0 or higher under favorable operating conditions. This represents a significant improvement in energy performance relative to electric resistance heating.

In addition to energy considerations, decentralized electric baseboard systems provide no cooling capability and offer limited opportunities for central monitoring or optimization. Temperature control and energy consumption vary between suites depending on occupant usage patterns. From a lifecycle perspective, while baseboard heaters have low mechanical complexity, the absence of centralized infrastructure limits system-level efficiency improvements.

Given the building’s age and the reliance on electric resistance heating, conversion to a heat pump–based system should be considered in the short to medium term as part of a broader modernization strategy aimed at improving energy efficiency, reducing operating costs, and providing integrated heating and cooling capability.

items.title: Absence of pipe insulation:
items.text:
Heating distribution piping in the mechanical room was observed to be uninsulated, resulting in avoidable heat loss and reduced system efficiency.

This condition presents an opportunity for low-cost energy efficiency improvement through the installation of proper pipe insulation on all accessible heating distribution piping.

items.title: Ceiling heating
items.text:
Space heating within individual suites is provided through a decentralized electric resistance heating system consisting of electric baseboard heaters and radiant ceiling heating panels.

The radiant ceiling system utilizes embedded electric heating elements within the ceiling assembly to provide heat through thermal radiation to interior spaces. Electric baseboard heaters provide supplementary convective heating as required. Each suite is equipped with wall-mounted thermostats, allowing occupants to manually control space temperature.

This configuration provides basic suite-level temperature control; however, electric resistance heating operates at a coefficient of performance (COP) of approximately 1.0, resulting in relatively high electrical energy consumption compared to modern heat pump–based systems. In addition, the absence of centralized monitoring, scheduling, or optimization limits opportunities for system-wide energy management and may contribute to inconsistent comfort conditions across suites.

items.title: Common area space heating
items.text: In Common areas, additional heating and cooling are provided by ceiling-mounted 4-way ceiling cassette indoor unit units. These units provide localized conditioning to maintain occupant comfort in high-traffic areas and are integrated within the ceiling space.
